**What you should be able to do after this meeting.** Name the trick in a figure built to mislead you, and redraw it honestly without losing the point. Then pitch your project in five minutes, on slides where every title is a claim.

## Where to read more

Zelazny, *Say It With Charts*, for the grammar of it. [Adams](https://doi.org/10.4135/9788132108498) ch. 16 on presenting.

## Session A · 2:05–3:15

Two halves. First, figures. Which figure answers which question, and why — distributions, time, space. The instinct to be curious about a dataset before you model it. Then the flip side: what figures hide through aggregation, scale, binning, projection and cherry-picked windows, and how to read a published figure for what it is not showing. Second, talking. A deck is an outline with pictures. One claim per slide, and the claim is the slide title, not a label. No bullet lists. What the first thirty seconds have to do, what the last thirty have to do, and what to do with a question you cannot answer — which is to say so.

## Session B · 3:35–4:30

Every session B opens with a ten-minute team check-in: what you did
since last week, what is stuck, and who is doing what next. Written
down, and handed in with that session's work.

Six figures, each lying a different way, one per team. A truncated axis. Two axes manufacturing a correlation. A cherry-picked window. An aggregate moving opposite to every subgroup. Area scaled by radius. Counts where you needed a rate. Name the trick, then redraw it honestly — and the honest version still has to make a point, which is the hard half nobody practises. Then the pitch. Five minutes per team, five slides, one topic sentence per slide, using the skeleton you wrote last week. The room's questions are aimed at where the argument jumps. Then you rate your teammates for the first time.

Your team's output is submitted before you leave.

## Due

Project pitch — one page, presented in class · Writing 1 — reverse outline · Rate your teammates
